brief.concept: Walk-up specialty coffee kiosk at a Barcelona metro exit selling flat whites at €3 for commuters, paid by card or app.
brief.for: Weekday commuters who walk through the exit between 7:30 and 9:30 and currently buy coffee elsewhere, or skip it.
brief.goal: Reach 60 paid pre-orders for pickup by week 4, or stop before spending on equipment.

checklist.task: Interview 20 commuters at the target metro exit
checklist.how: Stand near the exit on two weekday mornings and ask five questions about where they buy coffee, what they pay, and how long they wait.
checklist.done_when: 20 interviews logged, 8 or more say they buy coffee on the way in.

checklist.task: Count foot traffic and coffee carriers at two exits
checklist.how: Stand at each of two exits for 60 minutes on two peak mornings with a tally counter, recording people passing and people carrying cups from nearby cafés.
checklist.done_when: Counts logged for 2 exits across 2 peak mornings.

checklist.task: Price-check six cafés near the exit
checklist.how: Visit six cafés within about 300 metres of the exit and record flat white price, opening time, and whether they take takeaway orders.
checklist.done_when: 6 prices logged, with your €3 compared against each.

checklist.task: Launch a pay-now pickup order page
checklist.how: Publish a one-page order form with card checkout and a 7:30 to 9:30 pickup window, shared only with interview contacts.
checklist.done_when: Page live with working checkout and 3 completed test orders.

checklist.task: Run a two-morning paid pop-up at the exit
checklist.how: Confirm the council permit first, then sell flat whites at €3 from a borrowed machine and card reader for two morning shifts.
checklist.done_when: 40 or more cups sold across two mornings, at least 25 by card.

checklist.task: Ask every pop-up buyer about daily pre-orders
checklist.how: Ask each buyer one question: would you pre-order this for pickup on your usual commute, and at what time.
checklist.done_when: 15 buyers asked, 5 or more say yes to daily pre-orders.

checklist.task: Finalise the one-page offer and pickup sign
checklist.how: Write one line with the offer, price and pickup time, and put it on the order page and a printed sign using two colours and one photo.
checklist.done_when: Sign and page approved by 5 interview contacts.

checklist.task: Send 60 personal invites with the pickup link
checklist.how: Message friends, former colleagues and contacts who commute through the exit, asking for a pre-order at €3 with the pickup link.

checklist.task: Publish three posts in groups you already belong to
checklist.how: Post the offer, price and pickup window in three neighbourhood or commuter groups you already use, without buying ads.

checklist.task: Count paid pre-orders and decide go or stop
checklist.how: On day 28, export the payment report, total paid pre-orders for pickup, and compare the total against the gate of 60 before any equipment spend.
checklist.done_when: Paid pre-orders counted and compared with the gate of 60.

brief.summary: Barcelona had 1,729,963 registered residents on 1 January 2026, so the city has a large base of potential buyers. No source gives commuter counts, daytime workers or footfall at any metro exit, so the demand case for this exact spot is unproven. Named Barcelona shops list flat whites from €2.50 to €3.90, which places a €3 price inside the market range. The 10% VAT rate covers drinks for immediate consumption, including takeaway, so the €3 price includes VAT at 10%. Net revenue per cup is €€2.73, and contribution per cup is €€2.05. Fixed costs of about €€2,889 a month need 1,411 cups a month to break even. Startup capital is estimated at €€23,400. The biggest unknowns are site cost, kiosk permissions and whether commuters at this exit will buy at €3. Verdict: Test first (score 5.5/10). Main reason: €3 sits below Syra Coffee's €3.90 flat white and inside the €3–4.50 range that Barcelona Tourism gives for third-wave cafés (barcelonatourism.org, August 2026; no source id).

# Founder report: Barcelona metro-exit specialty coffee kiosk

## Executive summary

Barcelona had 1,729,963 registered residents on 1 January 2026 [S1], so the city has a large base of potential buyers. No source gives commuter counts, daytime workers or footfall at any metro exit, so the demand case for this exact spot is unproven. Named Barcelona shops list flat whites from €2.50 to €3.90, which places a €3 price inside the market range. The 10% VAT rate covers drinks for immediate consumption, including takeaway, so the €3 price includes VAT at 10% [S5][S7]. Net revenue per cup is €€2.73, and contribution per cup is €€2.05. Fixed costs of about €€2,889 a month need 1,411 cups a month to break even. Startup capital is estimated at €€23,400. The biggest unknowns are site cost, kiosk permissions and whether commuters at this exit will buy at €3. Verdict: Test first (score 5.5/10). Main reason: €3 sits below Syra Coffee's €3.90 flat white and inside the €3–4.50 range that Barcelona Tourism gives for third-wave cafés (barcelonatourism.org, August 2026; no source id).

## Verdict

**TEST FIRST** (score 5.5/10)

- €3 sits below Syra Coffee's €3.90 flat white [S4] and inside the €3–4.50 range that Barcelona Tourism gives for third-wave cafés (barcelonatourism.org, August 2026; no source id). Three Marks lists a flat white at €2.50 (guidavera menu, undated; no source id), so price pressure is real.
- The population is large, but no source counts the people who pass this exit or their buying habits. The city figures are for the whole city, not for the station [S1].
- Traditional bars charge €1.50–2.50 for a café con leche (barcelonatourism.org, 2026; no source id). Commuters can buy a cheaper drink nearby.
- The cost model points to fixed-cost absorption as the main risk: at low volume, fixed cost per cup rises fast (mycoffee.guide, 2025; estimate).
- Self-employed fees are known. The reduced fee is €80 a month for 12 months [S11], and the real monthly cost is €88.64 with MEI included [S12]. The rest of the costs are not known.

## 3 things to validate first

1. **Commuters at this exit will buy enough cups to cover fixed costs.**
   - *Why it matters:* If footfall is low, the kiosk cannot reach 1,411 cups a month, and the savings are lost.
   - *Test this month:* Stand at the exit for four weekday mornings and count people who pass, then offer a flat white at €3 with a sign and a card or cash option. Record cups sold each morning, then scale to a four-week monthly figure.
   - *Pass:* Sales of at least 1,411 cups a month, extrapolated from the test (estimate: using a pop-up with the same hours as the kiosk).

2. **Commuters will pay €3 instead of a cheaper bar or a €2.50 flat white.**
   - *Why it matters:* If buyers choose the €2.50 option or a bar, the price cannot cover the cost per cup.
   - *Test this month:* Offer two prices for two weeks, €3 and €2.50, and record the share of buyers who choose each.
   - *Pass:* At least 60% of buyers choose the €3 option at the €3 price (estimate: a threshold set by the founder, not from a source).

3. **Site, permit and fixed costs are known and fit the budget.**
   - *Why it matters:* A premises takeover in Barcelona can cost €70,000–80,000 (mycoffee.guide; estimate). A kiosk on transit land may cost less, but nothing in the research confirms this.
   - *Test this month:* Get written quotes for rent or concession fees, permit requirements and fit-out costs from the transit operator and the city council.
   - *Pass:* Total fixed costs at or below €€2,889 a month and startup capital at or below €€23,400, with no premises premium.

## Customers & demand

**Takeaway:** The city has a large, dense population, but nothing in the research shows how many people use this metro exit or whether they buy coffee. Demand is unproven.

**Evidence:**
- (+) Barcelona had 1,729,963 registered residents on 1 January 2026, the second highest figure in forty years [S1].
- (+) There are 684,077 households, with an average of 2.46 persons per dwelling [S1].
- (+) Eixample (277,353) and Sant Martí (253,139) are the most populated districts [S1].
- (−) Seven of ten districts saw a slight fall in residents in 2026 [S3]. The city total also fell slightly from the previous year [S2].
- (?) Commuter and daytime-worker counts for the metro exit were not found.
- (?) The neighbourhood (barri) population around the exit was not found, and the station has not been named.
- (?) The age, income and occupation profile of likely buyers was not found.

**What it means for you:** The city is large enough to support a coffee kiosk, but that says little about one exit. Ask for footfall at this exact station before you spend on a site. The city-wide population figures do not tell you how many buyers pass the kiosk each day.

**Next actions:**
1. Name the station and its barri, then find the nearest published passenger counts from the transit operator.
2. Stand at the exit for four weekday mornings and count passers-by in 15-minute blocks.
3. Ask three to five regular commuters what they pay for coffee and where they buy it.

## Competition & alternatives

**Takeaway:** Named shops sell flat whites from €2.50 to €3.90. The €3 price is in the middle of the range, but a cheaper bar or a bundle deal is close by. No kiosk at a metro exit was found in the research.

**Evidence:**
- (+) Syra Coffee in Gràcia lists a flat white at €3.90 and a cortado at €3.00 [S4]. This is the highest flat-white price found for a named Barcelona shop.
- (+) Barcelona Tourism gives a flat-white range of €3–4.50 for third-wave cafés and €3–5 for Skye Coffee Co in Sant Antoni (barcelonatourism.org, August 2026; no source id).
- (−) Three Marks in Fort Pienc lists a flat white at €2.50 (guidavera menu, undated; no source id). This is below the €3 target.
- (−) A café con leche costs €1.50–2.50 in traditional bars (barcelonatourism.org, 2026; no source id). Traditional bars may charge €1.20–1.50 for an espresso (eurovistatrips.com, May 2026; no source id), though quality varies.
- (−) Pasta Madre in the Gothic Quarter sells a coffee and a croissant for €1.60 (thespiritedexplorer.com, undated). Bicioci Bike Cafe in Gràcia sells a coffee-plus-croissant combo for under €3 (same source). These bundles set a value benchmark.

**What it means for you:** A €3 flat white is in the middle of the market, not at the bottom. A cheap bar or a bundle deal is the main alternative for a commuter. The kiosk needs a clear reason to pay €3, such as speed, quality or a loyalty offer, that the research did not test.

**Next actions:**
1. Visit the three nearest cafés and bars to the exit, and record their flat-white and espresso prices and their opening hours.
2. Ask a barista at one of those shops how many morning customers they serve in the 8 to 10 am window.
3. Test the €2.50 and €3 price options during the validation week, as set out above.

## Money

**Takeaway:** The VAT rate is clear and favourable. The rest of the money picture is mostly missing: no rent, wage, equipment or margin data was found. The unit economics below are estimates.

**Evidence:**
- (+) Drinks for immediate consumption, including made-to-order items, carry the 10% reduced VAT rate [S5].
- (+) The 10% rate also applies to takeaway drinks when served for immediate consumption [S7]. A 2026 secondary guide confirms that coffee falls under 10% in general [S6].
- (=) Supermarket coffee is taxed at the 4% super-reduced rate [S8]. Retail bags are taxed differently from a kiosk drink, so the rate does not carry over.
- (−) At 105 cups a day, a Barcelona specialty bar in 2025 had fixed costs of €3.20 per cup against €2.27 of revenue after VAT on a €2.50 coffee (mycoffee.guide, 2025; no source id). Volume is essential.
- (−) Taking over a viable commercial space can require paying the previous tenant €70,000–80,000 (mycoffee.guide; no source id).
- (?) Commercial rent, barista wages, equipment costs, ingredient prices and margins were not found.

**Unit economics**

The unit is one cup of flat white sold at €3.00 including VAT. Net revenue per cup is the price after VAT, based on the 10% rate [S5][S7]. Variable costs are ingredients, packaging and card fees, which are paid per cup. Ingredients and packaging are estimated at €0.63 per cup, from a 2025 cost model for a Barcelona specialty bar (mycoffee.guide; estimate). Card fees are estimated at €0.05 a cup (estimate).

Fixed monthly costs include rent (estimate), utilities (estimate), insurance (estimate), accounting (estimate), the reduced self-employed fee of €88.64 a month [S12], and the founder's own pay (estimate). Contribution per cup is net revenue minus variable costs. Break-even is fixed monthly costs divided by contribution per cup. Figures are computed in code and shown in the placeholders above.

## Risks & how to start

**Takeaway:** Self-employed registration is well documented, and a reduced fee is available. Permits, energy costs, failure rates and kiosk-specific rules were not found. The fee figures in the sources do not fully agree, so check them before budgeting.

**Evidence:**
- (+) New self-employed workers in Barcelona pay €80 a month for the first 12 months [S11]. This can be extended for 12 more months if net earnings stay below the minimum wage (SMI) [S11].

- (=) Digital time recording is required once you have employees (RD-ley 8/2019, per ERPiA's Barcelona guide) [S10].
- (=) Verifactu invoicing software applies to self-employed workers on direct estimation from 1 July 2027. A postponement to October 2028 has been announced but was not yet in the BOE at the time of writing [S10]. This is a software vendor's summary, so confirm with the tax agency.

**What it means for you:** Registering as self-employed is cheap for the first year, so the registration itself is not a barrier. Permits and site rules are the real risk, because they decide whether a kiosk can open at all. Do not commit savings until those rules are confirmed in writing.

**Next actions:**
1. Ask the city council and the transit operator, in writing, which permits a kiosk at this exit needs and how long they take.
2. Confirm the 2026 self-employed fee bracket and the MEI treatment with the Seguridad Social or a gestor.
